step1_interpretation.searchIntent: Diagnostic with a procedural tail. The reader can see the ring and wants it gone, but the deciding question is what the ring is MADE of — the removal method and the safe tool both change with the answer.
step1_interpretation.archetypeJustification: Considered C (Procedural) since the reader wants a cleaning method. Rejected: the removal steps are genuinely short, while the misidentification axis is load-bearing. A ring at the waterline can be oils (wipes off), calcium scale (does not), algae, or a stain in the surface — opposite treatments, and the wrong call means either scrubbing calcium with a degreaser forever or taking an abrasive pad to a gelcoat. §7A: 'the misidentification section usually carries the article.' It does here.

adjacenciesRequiringExplicitBoundaries.boundary: Foam = organics lowering surface tension in the water column. Scum ring = organics adhering at the air/water interface. State the relationship explicitly and link BOTH ways (§5 reciprocal requirement). This shared-cause framing is an asset, not a problem — neither competitor page makes the connection.

step3_serpGap.whoRanks: TroubleFreePool (forum), abgal (AU vinyl liner maker), a Facebook group, an Amazon listing, YouTube, Lo-Chlor (chemical maker), Reddit, InyoPools, TileShop, CalSpas (hot tubs).
step3_serpGap.whatTheyAllDo: Every ranking page is a cleaning-product pitch: here is a spray, a sponge, or a tile cleaner, scrub it. Several are literally product pages.
step3_serpGap.THE_GAP: Not one of them explains WHY the ring forms at exactly the waterline, or that its composition decides the treatment. Two consequences nobody covers: (1) people scrub calcium scale with a degreaser indefinitely because it looks like scum; (2) melamine/abrasive pads and acidic tile cleaners are recommended without surface constraints, on vinyl liners and fiberglass gelcoat where they cause permanent damage. One YouTube title hedges '(Not for Minerals!)' — the closest anyone comes, and it is in a video title.
step3_serpGap.secondEdge: The mechanism below reframes the whole problem: the ring is not a cleaning failure, it is a readout of a contaminant class chlorine handles badly. That reframing does not appear on page one at all.

step3_mechanism.claim: A scum ring marks the boundary of what chlorine can oxidize — it is not a sign of low chlorine.
step3_mechanism.detail: Orenda distinguishes natural organics (leaves, body oils, mucus, sweat), which chlorine oxidizes relatively easily, from SYNTHETIC bather products — deodorants, soaps, perfumes, body lotions, cosmetics, tanning oils, sunscreen — which it explicitly says are 'not easy for chlorine to oxidize.' Their words on the tile line: 'If you have a scum line on there, chlorine is falling short of fully removing the oils and organics that created it. In some cases, chlorine is incapable of finishing the job.'
step3_mechanism.whyItMatters: It inverts the standard response. An owner sees a ring, assumes dirty water, and shocks the pool. But the ring is made of the exact contaminant class extra chlorine is worst against, so shocking burns money and produces disinfection byproducts without touching it. The ring can sit there at textbook-perfect free chlorine.
step3_mechanism.supportingChemistry: Enzymes break the carbon chains into CO2, which off-gasses, leaving residue chlorine CAN oxidize — effectively lowering the energy required. Enzymes do not address metals or inorganic ammonia.
step3_mechanism.VENDOR_CAVEAT: Orenda sells enzyme products and the article's conclusion is 'use enzymes'. §3 names Orenda as citable T3 for original chemistry work, and the oxidation-vs-enzyme mechanism is sound and chemically checkable. But the product conclusion is an interested one. Write the mechanism; do NOT write 'buy enzymes' in Orenda's voice. Their '90% of oxidant demand' figure is a vendor claim — attribute it or omit it, do not state it as fact.
